passage:
Last summer my friend Elizabeth messaged that she couldn't come to my birthday because her family was going to her aunt's. I stared at the phone for a long time. Then I sent just one thing: 🙂
I meant, "Okay, I'm sad, but I'm trying to be fine." That smile felt heavy to type.
Elizabeth replied, "Yay, glad you're okay!! 😊"
I felt worse. She thought I didn't care at all.
The next day at school I told her the smile was a sad smile. Her eyes went big. "It looked happy to me! My mum sends that one when she's pleased."
Now we have a rule: if it's a sad smile, we add words. She even sent me a voice message singing on my birthday.
- Seema

qa.q: What did Elizabeth reply after Seema's smile?
qa.a: "Yay, glad you're okay!! 😊"

qa.q: What was Seema feeling when typing the smile, and why did it go wrong?
qa.a: Seema felt disappointed but was trying to act fine, so the smile carried sadness; Elizabeth read the same face as pleased, because that is what it means when her mum uses it.

qa.q: What small step did the two friends choose to avoid this mix-up?
qa.a: They agreed to add words when a smile is a sad one, so the emoji is not left to carry the whole feeling.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth probably feel when she learned what the smile meant?
qa.a: She was probably surprised and a little sorry, since she had cheerfully replied to what was really a sad message.

grounding: The narrator uses an emoji to show a mood, and a friend reads the same emoji differently, showing how emojis can be ambiguous.

Class note, Thursday, Class 6 project group
During the science project chat on the school tablets, Chinmay posted a long idea for the volcano model with three diagrams. Trisha replied with a single 👍.
A few minutes later Chinmay came to my desk looking deflated. "She doesn't like it. She just put a thumb."
I asked Trisha, without naming Chinmay. She looked puzzled. "The thumb means it's great! I was typing on the bus and had no time."
I brought them together. Chinmay said a thumb alone felt cold, like "okay, whatever." Trisha said at home everyone uses it for "yes, love it."
Next lesson I asked the whole class what the thumbs-up, the smiley and the heart mean to them. The answers were all different.
- Mr Fernandes

qa.q: How did Trisha reply to Chinmay's volcano idea?
qa.a: With a single 👍.

qa.q: What does Chinmay's deflated look suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: Chinmay felt hurt and discouraged, reading the lone thumbs-up as cold, as if Trisha did not like his work.

qa.q: What did Mr Fernandes do next, and why was it a good step?
qa.a: He brought the two together to explain their meanings and then asked the class what common emojis mean to each of them, showing that the same emoji can mean different things.

qa.q: How did Trisha see her own thumbs-up?
qa.a: To Trisha it was warm and positive, the way her family uses it, so she was surprised it came across as cold.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a child using an emoji as a feeling and a classmate reading it very differently.

Sunday
Usha Khala sent a video of her cat trying to jump onto the fridge and falling into the laundry basket. I laughed so hard my stomach hurt. I sent back 😭 because that's what everyone in my class sends when something is SO funny.
Ten minutes later Khala called Ammi. "Is Asif all right? He sent crying faces!"
Ammi handed me the phone and I had to explain that crying faces can mean laughing-crying. Khala went quiet and then laughed. "In my time crying meant crying!"
Now I feel a bit silly. I will send 😂 to Khala from now on, or just type "hahaha". With my friends the crying face is fine.
- Asif

qa.a: It was trying to jump onto the fridge and fell into the laundry basket.

qa.q: What was Usha Khala feeling when she called Ammi?
qa.a: Usha Khala felt worried and concerned, thinking Asif was upset because of the crying faces.

qa.q: What choice did Asif make to avoid another mix-up?
qa.a: Asif decided to send a laughing face or type "hahaha" to Khala, while keeping the crying face for friends who read it the same way.

qa.q: How might Ammi have seen the phone call?
qa.a: Ammi may have been surprised at first, then amused to see how one emoji could mean opposite things to Asif and his aunt.

grounding: A child uses crying emojis to show laughter, and an adult reads them as sadness, showing emoji ambiguity across people.

Nani's notebook, Tuesday
Jasleen has started sending me voice notes every morning on her way to school. I hear the auto horn, her giggle, and "Good morning, Nani ji, I'm wearing the red clips you gave!" A typed message never makes me smile like this.
This evening she was recording something for her friend Parveen. She was copying a new girl's way of talking and laughing. Before she pressed send, I asked, "If that girl heard this, how would she feel? And can Parveen send it on?"
Jasleen stopped. "Anyone can forward it," she said slowly. She deleted it and recorded a different one, telling Parveen about the dance practice instead.
I told her I was proud she thought first.

qa.q: What does Jasleen say in her morning voice note to Nani?
qa.a: "Good morning, Nani ji, I'm wearing the red clips you gave!"

qa.q: What might Jasleen have been feeling when she said "Anyone can forward it"?
qa.a: She probably felt uneasy and a bit ashamed, realising the recording could be passed on and hurt the new girl.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Nani asking questions instead of scolding worked, because Jasleen worked out the risk herself and chose a kinder message.

qa.q: How does Nani experience the morning voice notes?
qa.a: The voice notes make Nani feel close and happy, because she can hear warmth and small details a typed message would miss.

grounding: A caregiver's note shows a child sending warm voice notes and thinking before sending a recording that could be forwarded.

Friday night
Sabina moved to Guwahati last month and we're not allowed to call every day, so we send voice notes. Tonight she sent one singing our school song very badly, and I played it five times. Her voice made me feel like she was sitting on my bed.
I started a reply. I was going to tell her that Chhoden cried in class today after the test and everyone saw. Halfway through, I stopped. Sabina's cousin is in my class. What if Sabina plays it and her cousin hears? What if it gets forwarded?
I deleted it. Instead I recorded me and my little brother doing her song even worse. She sent back ten laughing faces.
- Pema

qa.q: How many times did Pema play Sabina's voice note?
qa.a: Five times.

qa.q: What made Pema stop halfway through the first reply?
qa.a: Pema felt worried that the voice note about Chhoden crying could be heard by Sabina's cousin or forwarded, which could embarrass Chhoden.

qa.q: What would you advise a child who wants to share news about someone else in a voice note?
qa.a: Pause and ask whether the person would be okay if it were forwarded; if not, share your own news instead.

qa.q: If you were Chhoden, what would you want Pema to do?
qa.a: You would want Pema to keep the crying private and not record it where others might hear.

grounding: A child sends warm voice notes to a friend and stops before recording something about another person that could be forwarded.

In the village near Kottayam, the new calf was born just after sunrise. Jomon ran with Appa's old phone to make a video for Kalyani Chechi, who worked in a hospital in the city.
"Chechi, look, she's standing! Her legs are like sticks!" he whispered, laughing.
Behind him Appa and the neighbour were arguing loudly about the fence. Jomon watched the clip back and heard every angry word. Chechi might show it to her friends, and they might send it on.
He walked to the far side of the shed, where only the hens were talking, and recorded again.
That night Chechi sent a voice note back. Her voice was soft and shaky. "Jomon, I miss home so much. Thank you for the calf."

qa.q: Where did Jomon go to record again?
qa.a: To the far side of the shed, where only the hens were talking.

qa.q: How did Kalyani Chechi seem to feel when she sent the voice note back?
qa.a: Her soft, shaky voice suggests she felt touched and homesick, missing the village and grateful for the calf video. 🥺

qa.q: What did Jomon do well before sending?
qa.a: He watched the clip back, noticed the argument could be forwarded, and chose to re-record in a quieter place.

qa.q: How might Appa feel if the first video had been sent?
qa.a: Appa might feel embarrassed if his argument about the fence was seen by strangers or passed around.

grounding: A child makes a warm video message and thinks before sending about whether recorded content could be forwarded.

Monday: Mahima's first tabla lesson with Jatin Sir. Her fingers slapped the drum like wet chapatis. "Na-dhin-dhin-na," Sir said. Mahima got it wrong six times and hid her hands in her lap.
Thursday: Every evening after homework she practised on a steel plate, whispering the bols. Her brother complained about the noise. Her fingers ached, but the "na" started to ring a little.
Three weeks later, at the building's Diwali evening, Mahima played the short piece she had learned. She missed one beat, then found it again. When she finished, Jatin Sir nodded once. Mahima's grin was so wide her cheeks hurt, and she kept tapping the beat on her knees all through dinner.

qa.q: What did Mahima practise on every evening?
qa.a: A steel plate.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling when she hid her hands in her lap on Monday?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and discouraged after getting the beat wrong six times.

qa.q: What helped Mahima improve, and what could she keep doing?
qa.a: Practising a little every evening, even with aching fingers, built her skill; she could keep a short daily practice to grow her confidence.

qa.q: How might Jatin Sir see Mahima's Diwali performance?
qa.a: His single nod suggests he was pleased with her progress, noticing she recovered after missing a beat.

grounding: Over three weeks, a child learns tabla through repeated practice and her music comes to carry pride and fun.

passage: "Shankar, you asked why I close my eyes when I dance. Come, sit. When Dolma Ama was small, in the settlement near Mysore, the older women taught us a dance from Tibet, a land my parents had left and I had never seen. At first I only counted steps and stamped too hard. My teacher laughed and said, 'Dolma, don't count. Think of your grandmother's village.' I didn't know the village. But I knew my Ama's face when she sang. So I danced to her face, every evening for a year. At the New Year festival, the old people cried while I danced. That's when I understood. My feet were carrying their longing, not just steps."

qa.q: Where did Dolma learn the dance as a child?
qa.a: In the settlement near Mysore.

qa.q: What was young Dolma feeling when the old people cried?
qa.a: She felt moved and understood, realising her dancing carried the elders' longing for home.

qa.q: What choice inside the story changed how Dolma danced?
qa.a: She chose to stop counting and dance to her Ama's face, practising every evening for a year, which gave her movement feeling.

qa.q: How might the teacher have seen young Dolma's stamping at first?
qa.a: The teacher saw she was trying hard but only counting, so she gently laughed and suggested thinking of something meaningful instead.

grounding: A grandmother recalls learning a traditional dance through repetition and discovering it carried longing and pride.

At the village Ramlila, Arnab played Lakshman. During his long speech to Ram, he noticed people shifting, a baby crying, and two men near the tea stall talking loudly.
His throat tightened. Were they bored of him?
Then he remembered what Mohit Bhaiya said in practice: "When they fidget, give them something to watch."
Arnab stepped forward, raised his bow high, and paused. The talking stopped. He finished the speech louder and slower. Some children in front sat up straight.
Afterward Mohit clapped his shoulder. "You saw them, and you fixed it."
Arnab grinned, but he said, "It was a long speech, na? Maybe they were just tired."

qa.q: What did Arnab do with his bow during the speech?
qa.a: He raised his bow high and paused.

qa.q: What was Arnab feeling when he noticed people fidgeting?
qa.a: He felt nervous and worried that the audience was bored of him.

qa.q: What small step helped Arnab regain attention?
qa.a: He added a strong gesture and a pause, giving the audience something to watch.

qa.q: Why might the audience have fidgeted even if Arnab was good?

grounding: A child performing in a village Ramlila notices fidgeting, adjusts his performance, and realises it isn't a judgment of him.

In the school play in Toronto, Jin had the funniest line: "My sock is alive!" At rehearsal it always got a big laugh. But on the night, silence. Jin's stomach dropped. Maybe she was terrible.
Backstage, Santiago whispered, "They were listening! Look, the grandpa in the front row is still smiling."
Jin peeked through the curtain. People were leaning forward, waiting.

Jin laughed. Maybe silence doesn't mean they don't like you.

qa.q: What was Jin feeling when her line got silence?
qa.a: Jin felt anxious and disappointed, worrying she was terrible.

qa.a: Santiago pointed out that the audience was listening and smiling, which helped Jin see silence as engagement.

Backstage at the music school in Seoul, Soo-ah's hands would not stop shaking. She pressed them between her knees. Her mouth felt as dry as paper, and the piano in the hall looked a mile away.
"Is it fear or excitement?" her teacher asked quietly. Soo-ah couldn't tell. Her heart was racing either way.
"Breathe with me. In for four, out for six." They did it three times. Her shoulders dropped a little.
When her name was called, she walked out and searched the rows. There was Abebe from her class, in the third row, giving a tiny thumbs-up.
Soo-ah sat, placed her fingers on the keys the way she had practised a hundred times, and began. The first notes wobbled. By the fourth line, her hands were steady.

qa.a: In the third row.

qa.q: What does Soo-ah's shaking and dry mouth suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: Soo-ah was most likely nervous, but the racing heart could just as well be excitement; even she could not tell which, as her teacher's question shows.

qa.q: Which things helped Soo-ah's body settle?
qa.a: Slow breathing with her teacher, the piece she had practised many times, and spotting Abebe's friendly face all helped her hands grow steady.

qa.q: What is it like for Abebe watching from the third row?

grounding: Before a recital, a child's shaking hands and dry mouth show nervous excitement, and breathing, rehearsal and a friendly face help her settle.

At the community centre's inter-school singing contest, Lokesh sat in the green room, sipping water again and again. His voice cracked when he tried a warm-up note.
"My throat's gone," he croaked. "I can't."
Vishal, the centre's music volunteer, pulled a chair close. "Hands on your belly. Breathe so your hands move, not your shoulders." Lokesh tried. Slow in, slower out.
"Now hum the first line. Just hum."
The hum came out wobbly, then smoother. Vishal grinned. "You've sung this at every practice for a month. Your voice knows it even when your brain panics."
On stage, Lokesh found Vishal at the side and kept glancing at him. His first note was thin, but by the chorus it filled the room.

qa.q: What did Vishal ask Lokesh to hum?
qa.a: The first line.

qa.q: Why did Lokesh say "I can't"?
qa.a: Lokesh felt panicky and scared because his voice cracked, and he believed his throat had gone; the dry voice may also have been nervous excitement before a big moment.

qa.q: What steps did Vishal use to calm Lokesh?
qa.a: Vishal guided belly breathing, then a gentle hum, and reminded Lokesh of a month of practice, which settled the body before singing.

qa.q: How might Vishal see the cracked voice in the green room?
qa.a: Vishal seems to see it as normal pre-stage nerves rather than a real problem, which is why the volunteer stays calm and practical.

grounding: A child's dry, cracking voice before a contest settles with slow breathing, reminders of rehearsal and a familiar face.

He drew a dove in the middle with the blue marker. Elizabeth, who had come from London for a term, looked over. "In my old school, we'd draw a rainbow for peace."

passage:
Everyone in Dilnaz's class had started wearing digital watches with flashing lights. Dilnaz's old one had a cracked strap.
"Khala, can I get a new watch?" she asked Rukmini Khala, who looked after her after school.
Rukmini frowned. The month's money was already stretched, and Eid shopping was next week.
"What kind of watch?"
"Like Reshma's. With lights."
Rukmini thought. "What colour do you like best?"
"Purple," Dilnaz said without thinking.
They went to the market that evening. The light-up ones were costly, but Dilnaz found a plain purple watch with a star on the face. She put it on and looked at it again and again.
"It's mine," she said. "Nobody else has this one."

qa.q: What colour did Dilnaz say she liked best?
qa.a: Purple.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz feeling when she said "It's mine"?
qa.a: She felt proud and happy to have a watch that was special to her, not just a copy of her friend's.

qa.q: How did Rukmini help Dilnaz balance her wish with the family's situation?
qa.a: She asked Dilnaz about her own taste and took her to choose a watch that fit within their means.

qa.q: How might Rukmini feel seeing Dilnaz so happy?
qa.a: Rukmini likely felt relieved and glad that Dilnaz found something she loved without stretching the family too much.

grounding: A child wants a watch like classmates, and an adult helps balance family budget with the child's own taste.

passage:
In the barbershop near their flat in Hyderabad, Naveen pointed at a poster of a spiky gel haircut. "That one. Everyone in my class has it now."
His mother, Alka, raised an eyebrow. "Spikes for school? Your principal will call me."
Naveen slumped in the chair. "I'll look like a baby if I don't."
The barber waited, scissors ready.
Alka thought for a moment. "How about short on the sides, a little longer on top? You can spike it on weekends."
Naveen looked at himself in the mirror, then nodded. When the barber finished, he ran his fingers through the top. "I can do spikes on Sunday!"
Alka smiled. "And neat on Monday."

qa.q: What haircut did Naveen point at?
qa.a: A spiky gel haircut.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling when he slumped in the chair?
qa.a: Naveen felt frustrated and worried he'd look babyish if he didn't match his classmates.

qa.q: What did Alka suggest to balance school rules and Naveen's wish?
qa.a: She suggested short sides and a longer top, so Naveen could spike it on weekends but look neat for school.

qa.q: How might the barber see the conversation?
qa.a: The barber probably saw it as a common family negotiation and waited patiently for them to agree.

grounding: A pre-teen wants a haircut like his peers, and his mother helps balance school rules with his taste.

passage:
At the government school in the village, every child wore the same blue uniform. Hansa liked that. No one could tell who was rich.
But on Monday, Vasudha came with new white shoes, not the usual black. And a bag with shiny zips.
At lunch, a group of girls crowded round her. "Where did you get them?" Hansa looked at her own dusty chappals and tucked her feet under the bench.
Vasudha saw. "My Mama sent them from the city," she said quietly. Then she added, "Your plaits are the best in class, Hansa."
Hansa smiled a little. She still thought about the shoes all afternoon.

qa.q: What colour were Vasudha's new shoes?
qa.a: White.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling when she tucked her feet under the bench?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and self-conscious about her dusty chappals compared with Vasudha's new shoes.

qa.q: What did Vasudha do that helped Hansa?
qa.a: She noticed Hansa's discomfort and paid her a kind compliment about her plaits.

qa.q: How might the other girls see Vasudha's shoes?
qa.a: They saw the shoes as special and exciting, a sign of something new, even though everyone wore the same uniform.

grounding: In a village school, a child notices that uniforms reduce difference but shoes and bags still signal status.

passage:
At the primary school in Manchester, every child had a blazer with a house badge. Lars was in Green House, Camila in Red. On sports day, the houses sat in coloured rows and cheered for their own.
Lars loved his green badge. It made him feel part of a team.
But in the lunch queue he noticed something else. Camila's trainers had flashing lights, and a group of boys kept asking where she got them. Lars looked at his old trainers with the grey laces.
"The uniform's the same," he said to Camila later. "But everyone still looks at shoes."
Camila shrugged. "My cousin gave me these. They're too big." She wiggled her toes. "But yeah. People notice."

qa.q: What house was Lars in?
qa.a: Green House.

qa.q: What was Lars feeling when he looked at his old trainers?
qa.a: He felt self-conscious and a little left out, noticing that others admired Camila's flashing shoes.

qa.q: What did Lars figure out about uniforms?
qa.a: That uniforms make children look the same, but they still notice and compare shoes and other small things.

qa.q: How might Camila feel about the attention on her trainers?
qa.a: Camila seemed a bit uncomfortable, since the trainers were a hand-me-down and too big, even though others noticed them.

grounding: At a school with uniforms and house badges, a child sees belonging but also notices status cues in shoes.

passage:
At the Saturday football club in the community centre, every player got a red jersey with a number. Vandana loved hers. It made her feel part of the team.
But Disha's jersey was faded and had a tear on the shoulder, because it had been her sister's.
In the changing room, a girl said, "Why is yours so old?" Disha went red and pulled her hair over the tear.
Vandana stepped closer. "Numbers are what matter. You're number seven, the best striker."
The coach heard and said, "Same team, same jersey. What counts is how you play."
Disha smiled a little and ran onto the field first.

qa.q: What number was Disha?
qa.a: Number seven.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling when she pulled her hair over the tear?
qa.a: Disha felt embarrassed and self-conscious about her old, torn jersey.

qa.q: How did Vandana and the coach help Disha?
qa.a: They reminded everyone that the jersey shows the team and how you play matters more than how new it looks.

qa.q: How might the girl who asked about the jersey see things differently after the coach spoke?
qa.a: She might realise that the team jersey is about belonging, not about having the newest one.

grounding: At a sports club, matching jerseys show membership, but children still notice and compare the condition of gear.

passage:
On my first day at the new school, I didn't know anyone. At morning assembly, the whole school stood in lines. When the anthem started, everyone stood still, hands at their sides. I kept shifting my feet.
Anjali, who was next to me, whispered, "Stand straight. Don't move till it ends."
I was confused. Why so serious?
After assembly, I asked her. She said, "It's to show we're one school, together." Then she told me her grandfather had fought for the country.
The next day, I stood straight and sang along. I felt part of something bigger.
- Varun

qa.q: What did Anjali whisper to Varun?
qa.a: "Stand straight. Don't move till it ends."

qa.q: What was Varun feeling during the first assembly?
qa.a: Varun felt confused and unsure, not understanding why everyone was so serious.

qa.q: What helped Varun find meaning in the ritual?
qa.a: Anjali explained that standing still for the anthem shows unity, and shared her grandfather's story, giving it personal meaning.

qa.q: How might Anjali see Varun's first-day fidgeting?
qa.a: Anjali probably saw it as normal for a new student and wanted to help the newcomer fit in.

grounding: A new child learns the meaning of standing still during the anthem after a classmate's explanation.

Morning assembly note, Monday
Bhavna lit the assembly lamp for the first time today. Her hands trembled as she struck the match, and it went out twice. The whole school waited.
Afterward she came to me. "Sir, why do we light the lamp every day? It's just fire."
I explained that the lamp is a sign of starting the day with light and learning, and that doing it together makes the school feel like one family.
Bhavna thought for a moment. "So it's like saying good morning to everyone at once?"
"Exactly," I said.
Tomorrow she has asked to light it again.
- Vijay Sir

qa.q: How many times did the match go out?
qa.a: It went out twice.

qa.q: What was Bhavna feeling when her hands trembled?
qa.a: She was nervous and self-conscious, with the whole school watching her light the lamp.

qa.q: How did Vijay Sir help Bhavna find meaning in the ritual?
qa.a: He explained the lamp as a shared start to the day with light and learning, which helped her connect it to something familiar.

qa.q: How might the other students feel waiting while the match went out?
qa.a: Some might have felt impatient or sympathetic, but the shared waiting also showed they were part of the ritual together.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a child nervously lighting an assembly lamp and learning its meaning through explanation.

passage:
Republic Day
Today the whole school stood in the ground at seven, in our whitest shirts. When the flag opened at the top of the pole, marigold petals fell out on the head boy. Then we sang the anthem. My arms got goosebumps when six hundred voices went together, even though the tune is slow. Ankita stood next to me, singing loudly and off-key.
Then came the pledge. I say it every day but I never think about it. It's just words that roll out.
At break I asked Ankita why we say it. She said, "It's a promise to be good to our country and the people in it." Then she said her father sometimes cries at the anthem on TV.
Tomorrow I'll listen to the words when I say them.
- Jomon

qa.q: What did Ankita say the pledge was?
qa.a: "It's a promise to be good to our country."

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling when everyone sang together?
qa.a: Jomon felt moved, with goosebumps, even without fully understanding the words.

qa.q: What helped Jomon understand the pledge?
qa.a: Asking Ankita and hearing her explanation and family story gave the ritual more meaning.

qa.q: How might Ankita see the anthem and pledge?
qa.a: Ankita sees them as a promise and something that brings strong feelings, even to her father.

grounding: A child on Republic Day feels the power of collective ritual and gains meaning through a friend's explanation.
